claims.claim: The last session of the council began on 3 December and ended on 4 December 1563
At the close Morone, first legate, blessed the synod and said 'go in peace'; they answered 'Amen'
The cardinal of Lorraine opened the acclamations, and the fathers answered
The acclamation 'let us confess the faith thereof, let us ever keep the decrees thereof' was answered 'Ever let us confess, ever keep'
'Anathema to all heretics' was answered 'Anathema, anathema'
Waterworth says Lorraine led and composed the acclamations, after the model of the ancient councils
Servanzio's diary, as Waterworth quotes it, says many shed many tears for great joy as they left
Paleotto, as Waterworth quotes him, says great wonder, applause and joy broke out at the acclamations
Pallavicino says faces all around were wet with tears
The acts are held in English in Waterworth's translation, from the bull of indiction to the bull of confirmation
Waterworth writes as a Catholic: the councils' prelates are 'secured from error, in matters of faith'
Waterworth calls Sarpi's history 'skilful, but unfair' and Pallavicino's 'laborious and authentic'
Sarpi was a Venetian friar of the Servite order
Sarpi writes against the papal power: the council confirmed the 'exorbitant power' of the See of Rome
Pallavicino was a Jesuit, later a cardinal, and wrote to refute a 'false' history issued under the name Pietro Soave Polano
Paleotto's and Servanzio's diaries are not held; they reach us in Waterworth's footnote and Pallavicino's citations
Paul III's bull of indiction was given at Rome on the eleventh of the calends of June 1542
Waterworth's note gives the bull's date as 22 May
The bull convoked a general council at Trent, to open on the calends of November 1542
The bull says the Germans 'wished for the city of Trent', though the pope thought Cisalpine Italy more convenient
The bull says the council was called 'principally on their account, and at their instance', in the city they desired
The bull says Christian unity was 'rent and well-nigh torn asunder by schisms, dissensions, heresies'; Rhodes lost, Hungary ravaged
The bull lists the council's business: religion, manners, the peace of princes, and repelling barbarians and infidels
The bull says Charles V had promised the dissenters his mediation
The bull says that at the diet of Regensburg the pope was asked to tolerate some dissenting articles until a council decided them
'Laetare Jerusalem' lifted the suspension and reconvened the council at Trent, dated 19 November 1544 (thirteenth of the calends of December 1544)
A papal brief set the opening for Gaudete Sunday, the third of Advent
Julius III recalled the council; the eleventh session met on 1 May 1551
Pius IV reconvened the council by his bull given at St Peter's in 1560
The first session was held on 13 December 1545, with a decree asking whether the council 'do begin, and hath begun'; 'It pleaseth us'
The opening decree names the extirpation of heresies, the peace of the Church, reform of clergy and people, and the enemies of the Christian name
Sarpi says the legates came 'with all the Prelates, in number 25' in procession to the cathedral
Pallavicino counts, besides three legates, the cardinal of Trent, four archbishops, twenty bishops, five generals, Pighini and Ferdinand's envoys
Waterworth gives Pallavicino's count and notes Le Plat's list has twenty-two bishops
The council met in three periods: ten sessions under Paul III, six under Julius III, nine under Pius IV
Sessions IX and X were held at Bologna in 1547, the tenth on 2 June
Waterworth counts 102 prelates besides the presidents at the first general congregation, 15 January 1562
Sarpi says 112 mitred prelates, besides the cardinals, walked in procession on 18 January 1562
In a letter Bonnet dates to January 1545, Calvin calls the pope Antichrist and the 'Romish idol'
Calvin foresees his side refusing to entrust religion to 'the professed enemies of God': 'they will never permit him to be the judge'
Bonnet says the 1545 letter has no address and no date
Waterworth dates the public audience of the Württemberg and Saxon envoys to 24 January 1552
Sarpi says Badehorn spoke for Maurice of Saxony and asked for a safe-conduct like Basel's, citing a decree of Constance
Sarpi gives the Saxon terms: a 'general, free, and Christian Council' deciding controversies 'according to the Holy Scripture'
Sarpi says the Saxons asked that the council 'first repeat, approve, and ratifie the Article of the Superiority of the Council above the Pope'
Waterworth says the envoys demanded that the decrees of Basel and Constance limiting papal authority be approved
Sarpi says the Württemberg envoys asked for judges chosen by both sides, since neither plaintiff nor defendant should judge
Jewel calls it 'a conspiracy and not a council'
Jewel's Apology was first published in 1562; Jewel was bishop of Salisbury
Jewel: 'we have not tarried for ... the authority or consent of the Tridentine council'; 'not one of our divines could be heard'
Calvin, 10 April 1551, to Bullinger: 'We may accordingly remain at home.'
Bonnet says the Reformed cantons refused to send deputies
Bonnet says Calvin answered the decrees in his Antidote of 1547
Sarpi's frame: a convocation 'procured and hastened' by some, 'hindered and deferred for the space of 22 years' by others
claims.note: OCR 'deterred' and '2.2.' (S l.8790); read as 'deferred' and '22'

claims.claim: Session IV, 8 April 1546: truth is in the written books and the unwritten traditions 'transmitted as it were from hand to hand'
Session IV receives Scripture and traditions 'with an equal affection of piety, and reverence'
Session IV declares the old Vulgate 'authentic' and forbids interpreting Scripture against the Church's sense
Session VI, 13 January 1547: faith is 'the beginning of human salvation, the foundation, and the root of all Justification'
Canon IX condemns justification by faith alone 'in such wise as to mean that nothing else is required to co-operate'
Waterworth says chapter VII is directed mainly against Luther's errors and also aims at Seripando's opinion
Session VIII, 11 March 1547: the disease 'so plainly and notoriously certain' that the council was transferred 'for a time' to Bologna
Session XV, 25 January 1552: the safe-conduct promises not to use any councils, 'especially those of Constance and Sienna', against it
Session XV notes that the Protestants 'have not as yet come'
Session XVI, 28 April 1552, suspended the council; it 'irritated rather than calmed the minds of many'; German bishops had withdrawn
Session XVII, 18 January 1562: business to be what 'the Legates and Presidents proposing' seemed fit
Session XXIII, 15 July 1563: pastors are 'by divine precept' bound to know their sheep; all over churches, even cardinals, must reside
Waterworth's note: the word 'Assistunt' was long opposed by those who denied residence to be of divine right

Session XXIII, chapter XVIII: cathedral churches to train youths of at least twelve in a college, the poor chosen first; the bishop assigns some to the churches, keeps the rest, and fills the places of those withdrawn, 'that so this college may be a perpetual seminary of ministers of God'
Session XXV: 'no hope remains' the heretics will come; the earlier decrees were recited; the fathers voted to close and ask confirmation
Session XXV sent the Index, catechism, missal and breviary to the pope for completion
Sarpi says Monte 'suborned some to ask the Physicians, whether those Infirmities were not Contagious'
Pallavicino says Sarpi asserts the papal order 'senza veruna prova'
Pallavicino says spotted fever with unusual deaths struck Trent; the bishop of Capaccio died three days after the session
Pallavicino quotes Fracastoro, the council's physician, swearing before the notary he would not stay another month in Trent
Sarpi says 35 bishops and three generals agreed to the transfer, Pacheco and 17 others opposed
Pallavicino says of 56 present, 38 approved, 14 opposed, two were doubtful and two conditional
Sarpi gives the vote of 20 April 1562 as 68 placet, 33 non placet, 13 and 17 deferring to the pope
Pallavicino says the opponents were 38 or 37 and the middle 34, so most would not define without the pope
Pallavicino quotes the council secretary's tally: 66 affirmative, later 67 with Lérida's vote
Pallavicino cites Paleotto's acts, Servanzio's diary and the Florentine ambassador's letters on the vote
Waterworth says Granada and Orense protested 'the Legates and presidents proposing', and Leon and Almeria agreed conditionally
Sarpi says four prelates contradicted the words, naming Guerrero of Granada, Bianco of Orense, della Questa of Leon and the bishop of Almeria
Sarpi says the fathers answered 'not one by one, but altogether, Placet' (OCR 'now')
Pallavicino says the archbishop of Granada alone would not ask confirmation, and three Spanish bishops asked it 'come necessaria'
Waterworth says all voted for both proposals except Granada
The acts count 255 signers: four legates, two cardinals, three patriarchs, 25 archbishops, 168 bishops, seven abbots, 39 proctors, seven generals
The count is certified by Massarelli, secretary, and two notaries
Pallavicino gives 255 signers and 168 bishops
Waterworth gives 255 signers and 168 bishops
Sarpi prints '268 Biſhops' among otherwise matching figures
Waterworth says Luna would not sign without the clause 'provided the Catholic King consent'; the envoys' acceptances were drawn up apart within two days
Pallavicino says Luna would sign only with the king's assent reserved, and the envoys' acceptances were taken apart
Sarpi gives the French ambassador's absence and Luna's reservation as the two reasons the ambassadors did not sign
Waterworth prints Le Plat's lists of those present in the first ten sessions and in the nine under Pius IV
Mansi prints names of the fathers at Bologna and at session XI
Sarpi calls Lorraine's leading the acclamations 'a lightness and vanity not beseeming such a Prelate'
Pallavicino says Lorraine composed the acclamations like the ancient councils', and seemed to grant Pius a supremacy the French had disputed
In consistory on 26 January 1564 Pius IV, with the cardinals' 'advice and assent', confirmed all the council's decrees
Pius IV's bull of confirmation is dated the seventh of the calends of February 1564 (Waterworth: 26 January)
Mirbt titles the bull 'Benedictus Deus' and dates it 26 January 1564
The bull forbids publishing commentaries on the decrees without papal authority and reserves doubts to the Apostolic See
Pallavicino says that in the consistory the pope asked the cardinals' votes and confirmed by common consent
Sarpi says most of eight cardinals wanted the decrees moderated before confirmation
Sarpi says Amulio, 'in whose Memorials I have seen this negotiation', urged confirming at once
Sarpi says Monte, the prime legate, sang the Mass of the Holy Ghost at the opening
Sarpi says Monte proposed the transfer in the general congregation
Le Plat's list names Joannes Maria de Monte, later Julius III, and Marcellus Cervinus among the first legates
Le Plat's list names Christophorus Madrucius, cardinal and bishop of Trent
Sarpi says Madruzzo would not answer the residence question precisely
Waterworth says Lainez argued ably against the system of intrinsic and extrinsic justice
Sarpi says Lainez spoke more than two hours that jurisdiction was given wholly to the bishop of Rome
Le Plat's list for 1562 names Hercules Gonzaga first among the presidents
Sarpi says Mantua said the greater number demanded a declaration, and Simonetta favoured residence de jure positivo
Morone and Simonetta petitioned Pius IV for confirmation in consistory
Giussano names Gabriel Paleotto, auditor of the Rota
Waterworth names Angelo Massarelli as secretary
Mirbt dates the bull 'Iniunctum nobis' and the Professio fidei Tridentinae to 13 November 1564
The Profession swears 'veram obedientiam' to the Roman pontiff and receives what Trent defined
McHugh and Callan say Pius V, elected 17 January 1566, had the Catechism revised; its first edition was printed at Rome in 1566
Giussano says Pius IV gave his nephew Charles the oversight of the council's business
Giussano says Trent's decrees were 'read and formally accepted' at Milan's first provincial council, 15 October 1565
At the session of 17 September 1562 Amulio's letter on Abdisho, patriarch of Muzal in Assyria, was read
Pallavicino gives the reading of Abdisho's profession at session XXII
Abdisho's profession is dated Rome, 7 March 1562
Abdisho swore at Rome before Amulio that he could not come to the synod but would teach what Trent would settle
Amulio's letter, Rome, August 1562, says Abdisho came to Rome 'the year before' and stayed months
Amulio's letter says Abdisho would have gone to the council had he not hastened home
Sarpi dates Abdisho's profession 17 March
Sarpi says the Parliament's counsellors in France opposed the reform articles
Sarpi: 'the Princes of Germany held none esteem of this Council'
The editors of Ignatius's letters say Laynez and Salmerón came to Trent on 18 May 1546 as the pope's theologians
Ignatius sent instructions for the journey to Trent, Rome, early 1546
Le Plat's list says Pole left before the fifth session
Pius IV's bull calls the gathering 'a most numerous assembly of bishops', from all the nations of Christendom
Sarpi judged the council made the discords 'irreconcileable'
Pallavicino says they saw finished after eighteen years a work thorny with labours, hard with difficulties and rich in fruit
The canons on baptism condemn rebaptism without naming the Anabaptists

Pallavicino gives the audience of the Württemberg and Saxon envoys: the Württemberg men handed their Confession to the secretary, and he sums up the Saxons' petitions in five heads, the fourth that the pope be declared subject to the council before all else

Luther's Smalcald Articles, dated 1537 in the edition, were written for the council Paul III had called to Mantua, before Trent met; they were to be presented if the pope held 'a truly free Christian Council', and say 'the Romish court is so dreadfully afraid of a free Christian Council'
Paul III's bull of 1542 says he had called the council to Mantua for 1537, was refused the city, and chose Vicenza and then Trent
The Lutheran Formula of Concord says 'the decree of the Council of Trent ... should by right be rejected', namely 'that our good works support salvation'; its Epitome is signed at Bergen, 29 May 1577
claims.note: Jacobs's footnote refers the decree to Sess. VI, can. XXIV (l.31038); the reference is the editor's.

claims.claim: Pallavicino says some officials of the Roman court advised the pope against an absolute confirmation, since it cut the court's revenue and authority, and Boncompagni, Paleotto and many others opposed them
Waterworth counts, at the session of 18 January 1562, besides the cardinals, 106 bishops, four mitred abbots and four generals of orders
Giussano gives a round 'two hundred and fifty Bishops' assembled for the third period

contested_claims.claim: Whether the disease at Trent in 1547 was real or a pretext for the move to Bologna
contested_claims.sides: Real, 'plainly and notoriously certain': the acts (council-of-trent_canons-and-decrees_waterworth1848.txt l.14686-14688); Pallavicino, citing deaths and Fracastoro's oath (pallavicino_istoria-del-concilio-di-trento-parte2-ita_1664.txt l.4933-4937, 5366-5372) | Spread on purpose: Sarpi, Monte 'suborned some to ask the Physicians' (sarpi_history-of-the-council-of-trent_brent1676.txt l.28743-28747)
contested_claims.note: Pallavicino says Sarpi asserts the papal order without proof (P2 l.4928-4931).

contested_claims.claim: The vote on the transfer, 11 March 1547
contested_claims.sides: 35 bishops and three generals for, Pacheco and 17 others against: Sarpi (sarpi_history-of-the-council-of-trent_brent1676.txt l.28872-28876) | Of 56, 38 for, 14 against, 2 doubtful, 2 conditional: Pallavicino (pallavicino_istoria-del-concilio-di-trento-parte2-ita_1664.txt l.5570-5575)

contested_claims.claim: The vote on residence by divine right, 20 April 1562
contested_claims.sides: 68 for, 33 against, 13 and 17 deferring to the pope; the greater part approved: Sarpi (sarpi_history-of-the-council-of-trent_brent1676.txt l.45897-45915) | Near seventy for, 38 or 37 against, 34 between; most would not define without the pope; secretary's tally 66, then 67: Pallavicino (pallavicino_istoria-del-concilio-di-trento-parte2-ita_1664.txt l.47484-47555)
contested_claims.note: The decree of 15 July 1563 speaks of a 'divine precept' and does not define divine right (W l.19390-19414).

contested_claims.claim: Who objected to 'the Legates and Presidents proposing', 1562
contested_claims.sides: Granada and Orense protested; Leon and Almeria agreed on a condition: Waterworth (council-of-trent_canons-and-decrees_waterworth1848.txt l.7175-7181) | All four contradicted: Sarpi (sarpi_history-of-the-council-of-trent_brent1676.txt l.43979-43986)

All answered together, 'Placet': Sarpi (sarpi_history-of-the-council-of-trent_brent1676.txt l.70106-70110) | Votes taken one by one; Granada alone would not ask confirmation; three bishops asked it 'as necessary': Pallavicino (pallavicino_istoria-del-concilio-di-trento-tomo3-libri17-24-ita_classici-sacri1846.txt l.57578-57604); Granada alone: Waterworth (council-of-trent_canons-and-decrees_waterworth1848.txt l.11124-11131)

contested_claims.claim: How the cardinals in Rome received the decrees before confirmation
contested_claims.sides: Confirmed with the cardinals' 'advice and assent': the acts (council-of-trent_canons-and-decrees_waterworth1848.txt l.24171-24174); by common consent, after some officials of the Roman court had advised against an absolute confirmation: Pallavicino (pallavicino_istoria-del-concilio-di-trento-tomo3-libri17-24-ita_classici-sacri1846.txt l.57848-57867, 58030-58039) | Most of eight cardinals wanted them moderated first; Amulio urged confirming at once: Sarpi (sarpi_history-of-the-council-of-trent_brent1676.txt l.70324-70327, 70376-70416)

'A lightness and vanity not beseeming such a Prelate': Sarpi (sarpi_history-of-the-council-of-trent_brent1676.txt l.70194-70199) | Composed in the manner of the ancient councils, seeming to grant the pope a supremacy the French had disputed: Pallavicino (pallavicino_istoria-del-concilio-di-trento-tomo3-libri17-24-ita_classici-sacri1846.txt l.57627-57640)

7 March 1562: the print (abdisho-iv_approbatio-et-professio-fidei-concilio-tridentino-lat_1562.txt l.209); Pallavicino's note (pallavicino_istoria-del-concilio-di-trento-tomo3-libri17-24-ita_classici-sacri1846.txt l.9619) | 17 March: Sarpi (sarpi_history-of-the-council-of-trent_brent1676.txt l.51655)

contested_claims.claim: The number of bishops who signed
contested_claims.sides: 168: the acts (council-of-trent_canons-and-decrees_waterworth1848.txt l.24111-24116), Pallavicino (pallavicino_istoria-del-concilio-di-trento-tomo3-libri17-24-ita_classici-sacri1846.txt l.57682-57688), Waterworth (council-of-trent_canons-and-decrees_waterworth1848.txt l.11172-11174) | 268: Sarpi as printed (sarpi_history-of-the-council-of-trent_brent1676.txt l.70214-70215)
contested_claims.note: Sarpi's other figures match the acts, so 268 is probably a misprint or OCR error for 168; the page image is not checked. Not a real dispute; the acts' count stands.

contested_claims.sides: 'with all the Prelates, in number 25': Sarpi (sarpi_history-of-the-council-of-trent_brent1676.txt l.18406-18407) | cardinal of Trent, four archbishops, twenty bishops, five generals, besides three legates: Pallavicino (pallavicino_istoria-del-concilio-di-trento-parte1-ita_1664.txt l.35131-35135) | four archbishops, twenty-two bishops, five generals: Le Plat, as Waterworth reports (council-of-trent_canons-and-decrees_waterworth1848.txt l.3552-3554)
contested_claims.note: Pallavicino's cardinal of Trent, four archbishops and twenty bishops make 25 besides the legates, so he and Sarpi agree if Sarpi's 25 leaves the legates out. Le Plat's twenty-two bishops differ by two.

absent_details.detail: The eyewitness diaries and acts of Massarelli, Paleotto and Servanzio
absent_details.note: Not held. ls cic/texts | grep -i -E 'massarel|paleot|servanz|le-plat|leplat|theiner|concilium-tridentinum|goerres|ehses|merkle' found nothing. Paleotto and Servanzio reach us in Waterworth's footnote (W l.11159-11165) and Pallavicino's citations (P2 l.47532-47536).

absent_details.detail: The Württemberg Confession handed in at Trent in 1552, and any Saxon confession
absent_details.note: Not held. grep over all cic/texts for 'Confessio (Virt|Wirt)embergica|Wirtembergic|Confessio Saxonica|Repetitio confessionis|Saxon Confession|Wurtemberg Confession' gave no relevant hit; the name Badehorn occurs only in Sarpi, and Pallavicino tells the Saxon speech without it. Pallavicino says the Württemberg envoys handed their Confession to the secretary (P2 l.22388-22390). Their speeches reach us through Sarpi, Pallavicino (P2 l.22383-22660) and Waterworth.

absent_details.detail: Calvin's Acta Synodi Tridentini cum Antidoto (1547)
absent_details.note: Not held. Searched calvin_* and rilliet_* for 'antidot', 'Trident', 'Trent': only Bonnet's notes (C2 l.6728-6731, 7336-7341). Calvin's Opera vol. 7 is not vendored.
Not held. ls grep 'chemnitz|kemnitz|examen'; grep 'Examen Concilii|Examinis Concilii|Examination of the Council' over all cic/texts: only a bibliographic mention in an unrelated file.

The acts give the count without the names (W l.24105-24116). Le Plat's lists in Waterworth are of those present at any session of the first and third periods (W l.24409-24416, 25697-25703). Mansi's lists for Bologna and session XI were not counted.
